strengths: The paper targets an important and timely bottleneck: efficient long-context decoding under KV-cache memory pressure, especially when retrieval methods preserve accuracy better than dropping methods.

The core idea of speculative KV retrieval from adjacent decoding steps is simple, plausible, and well motivated by query-similarity measurements; the fine-grained correction mechanism is a reasonable safeguard against accumulated errors.

The work combines algorithmic and systems contributions, including group-consistent selection, hybrid CPU/GPU KV layouts, and double-buffered streamed recall, and the ablations indicate that these choices materially improve latency.

The empirical scope is stronger than many KV-cache papers: multiple model families, long-input, long-generation, and reasoning tasks, plus comparisons to several recent dropping and retrieval baselines.

Accuracy results are generally convincing at a high level: FreeKV is usually close to full KV and often among the best compressed methods, while latency gains over offloading-based retrieval baselines are large in the tested settings.
weaknesses: The efficiency evaluation is too narrow for the strength of the claims: it uses only one A100 PCIe platform, mainly 7B/8B models, limited batch sizes, and no production serving throughput, multi-request scheduling, H100/NVLink, or larger 70B-scale experiments despite those being central motivations.

The largest speedups appear to come from general system optimizations such as hybrid layouts, but the baselines are not shown with comparable optimized layouts or streamed recall; this makes it hard to know how much of the advantage is specific to FreeKV versus engineering that could also improve ArkVale, ShadowKV, or InfiniGen.

The paper claims O(B) GPU memory, but FreeKV also keeps page summaries on GPU and the full KV cache in CPU memory, both scaling with context length; the memory accounting and scalability discussion are therefore incomplete.

Near-lossless accuracy is somewhat overstated. Several reported gains over full KV are likely within stochastic/evaluator noise, yet there are no confidence intervals, repeated-seed statistics for all settings, or calibration of the LLM-based LongGenBench evaluator.

Reasoning tasks have high correction rates, sometimes around half the steps, but the paper reports accuracy without corresponding latency measurements for these hard reasoning workloads; this leaves the main accuracy-efficiency tradeoff under-tested where correction is most active.

Several baselines are modified to enforce group consistency or long-generation support, but the paper gives limited evidence that these adaptations are faithful or optimally tuned, raising concerns about comparison fairness.

Important sensitivity analyses are limited: budget, page size, sink/window size, correction threshold, CPU bandwidth pressure, and context lengths beyond the tested range are not explored enough to support broad deployment claims.

Reproducibility is weaker than expected: the abstract says code is available but the manuscript appears to contain only a placeholder marker, and implementation details for the controller, stream scheduling, and baseline modifications are not sufficient to reproduce the system confidently.
